To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cosmic microwave background constrains radiatively decaying cold dark matter to have a lifetime longer than 5.5×10^25 s (95% C. L.).
we have used the WMAP 3 year data combined with galaxy survey data to derive new constraints on dark-matter decay, which are 10 times stronger that previous limits.
we have derived new constraints on dark-matter decay to electromagnetic particles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interaction between dark-matter particles and the cosmic microwave background, with the aim of placing constraints on the decay of dark matter.
the study of the cosmic microwave background and its relation with dark matter.

the possibility that a fraction of the dark matter is composed of particles that decay into electromagnetic radiation, and that such radiation can affect the recombination process and the reionization process, and thus leave an imprint on the CMB.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dark matter is stable on cosmological timescales.

we have excluded the possibility of a significant contribution of decaying dark-matter particles to the CMB anisotropies, and that we are now in a position to probe the possibility that the dark-matter particle has a lifetime of the order of a few times 10^26 s.
dark matter is not radiatively decaying.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have constrained the dark matter decay rate to be below the rate of the proton decay.
we can now constrain dark-matter decay to photons and leptons to be less than a few percent of the total dark matter density.
dark matter cannot be a radiatively decaying particle with a lifetime longer than 10^8 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dark-matter decay to electromagnetically active particles cannot be the dominant source of the ionizing background in the Universe.
the WMAP data combined with galaxy survey data are a powerful probe of radiative dark-mater decay.
the Planck satellite should be able to rule out radiative decays as the dominant dark-matter decay mechanism.
